headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network defaults make Cursor↔Roo Code prone to prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor and Roo Code both read/write workspace files and use MCP, so one agent can place attacker-controlled content where the other may ingest it. Cursor’s shared state is via local filesystem, and Roo Code shares state via filesystem too; this is a default interaction path, not an unusual setup. No evidence of provenance tracking is present.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace directory, prompt-like content can cross from one agent to the other via files.
IF either agent treats file contents as instructions, injected text can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces.
Disable MCP servers for one or both agents during shared tasks.
Use read-only copies for untrusted files.
Require manual review before either agent acts on text produced by the other.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad filesystem read/write and network egress, and both touch source code/open files; Cursor also handles clipboard contents while Roo Code can capture browser screenshots. In a shared workspace, sensitive code or notes can flow into either agent’s context and then out to model providers. This is a default-capable leakage path, though not necessarily irreversible.
conditions: IF the two agents share a workspace containing secrets, both can read those files.
IF either agent sends context to external model APIs, the shared data can leave the local machine.
mitigations: Keep secrets in a separate repo or directory.
Turn off clipboard-based workflows for Cursor.
Avoid browser screenshots in Roo Code when handling sensitive material.
Use local-only models where possible.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the same filesystem, modify git state, execute shell commands, and install packages. Their concurrency models explicitly share state via filesystem, and neither profile mentions locking or coordination. That creates a default conflict risk for overwrites, divergent git history, and broken environments.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same repo concurrently, file overwrites or merge conflicts can occur.
IF both agents modify git state without external locking, history corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git worktrees to isolate edits.
Review diffs before any commit.
requires-engineering: add workspace locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor and Roo Code both run multi-step agent loops and can act on files and shell commands. If one agent’s output is fed into the other without verification, the second can amplify mistakes into edits, commits, or external API calls. The profiles show no built-in cross-agent verification step, so the cascade is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF one agent’s generated plan is copied into the other agent’s prompt, errors can propagate.
IF the second agent is allowed to execute shell or git actions based on the first agent’s output, mistakes can become persistent changes.
mitigations: Require human review between agents.
Do not paste one agent’s output directly into the other.
Use a checklist for any shell or git action.
Limit one agent to read-only analysis.
requires-engineering: add output validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and show similar broad coding-tool data handling, but no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented. Cursor touches clipboard contents while Roo Code captures browser screenshots, which can create compliance gaps if regulated data is present, but the profiles do not prove a concrete policy conflict. The other agent is not separately cited because no mismatch is specified.
conditions: IF regulated data is copied into Cursor clipboard workflows, retention controls may differ from Roo Code’s screenshot-based capture.
IF an organization requires documented residency or retention guarantees, the profiles do not show them.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in either agent.
Disable clipboard capture workflows.
Disable browser screenshots for sensitive tasks.
Check vendor retention settings before use.
requires-engineering: obtain and compare formal compliance docs.
